SMTO-FIL-0032 — SMTO can't confirm whether the copied file was saved

GUID: 627c8ae4-b66e-4651-9b6f-14b3cddaa690
Slug: file-invalid-commit-receipt
Domain: FIL · Subsystem: files

What happened

  • A copy between Gateways reached its last step, but the receiving computer's reply didn't match what SMTO expected. The file may or may not have been saved at the destination.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask SMTO in the conversation to show the size and last-modified time of the file at the destination and of the original file, and compare them. If the destination file is already there and matches, the copy doesn't need to be repeated.
  2. Only if the destination file is missing, or clearly differs from the original, ask SMTO to copy it again. Copying again without checking could overwrite a file that already arrived correctly.
  3. If you can't tell whether it arrived, open Technical details and select Copy error details. The details hold the copy's number and destination path, which are needed to check it on the Gateway.

What success looks like

  • The destination file exists with the same size as the original, or a new copy finishes with a verified result.

If it still fails

  • Send the copied error details to the person who manages the destination Gateway and ask them to verify the file there. Don't keep repeating the copy until someone has confirmed what happened to the first one.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Gateway copy sent destination_commit, but the reply lacked status 'committed', a matching SHA-256 or size, or a valid f1 revision; publication may already have happened, so the outcome is recorded as unknown_effect.

What this means

  • The destination commit reply lacks committed status, matching SHA-256/size or a valid bounded f1 revision, after commit may already have published. File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.

Why this can happen

  • The destination commit reply lacks committed status, matching SHA-256/size or a valid bounded f1 revision, after commit may already have published.

How to diagnose it

  • Reconcile the original transfer and actual destination identity/hash; do not manufacture a receipt or repeat commit.

How to fix it

  • Do not replay destination_commit. On the destination Gateway, run destination_status or destination_reconcile for the transfer_id with the relay's SHA-256 and size, or compare the destination file's size and SHA-256 with the source, before any further write; also compare controller and Gateway versions for a protocol mismatch.
  • Reconcile the original transfer's destination and receipt before any further write; do not replay commit.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect and reconcile authoritative state before repeating any mutation or control request. Do not blindly retry.

How to verify the fix

  • Supported reconciliation proves the original publication or retains its uncertainty.

What not to do

  • Do not repeat a mutation while the earlier outcome or current owner is unresolved.

Technical notes

  • File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
